# Hitopadesha

-> 140 <-

Since the time for war <note>original: <term>vigraha</term></note> has arrived, why does the King not prepare for battle beforehand? For it is said: What kind of servant or what kind of minister is he who, without any consideration, directs the King toward military engagement and the abandonment of his own position at the very beginning?

Furthermore: One should strive to conquer enemies by any means other than war. Victory is seen to be uncertain when two sides are fighting.

And another thing: One should strive to overcome the enemy through conciliation <note>original: <term>sama</term></note>, gifts <note>original: <term>dana</term></note>, or sowing dissension <note>original: <term>bheda</term></note>, used either separately or all together; but never through war.

Moreover: Every person is a hero as long as they have not encountered a real conflict. Who is not prideful before they have witnessed the strength of the opponent?

Additionally: A great result is not achieved by creatures through harsh means as effectively as it is through mild efforts. Achievement comes from small means. However, seeing that war is at hand, let it be regarded with caution <note>original: <term>avajñīyatām</term> suggests looking down upon or treating it with strategic disregard</note>. For it is said:

When the battle is imminent, the Chakravaka <gloss>ruddy sheldrake or Brahminy duck, serving here as a wise minister</gloss> says: O Great King, war is not the first duty. What kind of servant or minister is he who advises the King to prepare for battle and leave his own place without prior deliberation? Furthermore, one should try to defeat the enemy through conciliation and other peaceful means; never by battle. This is because between two combatants, it is not known for certain who will be the victor. Furthermore, one should strive to resolve the enemy through conciliation, gifts, or dissension, either individually or collectively; never through war. Furthermore, all people are brave as long as they have not fought.

<summary>The minister Chakravaka advises the King against jumping into immediate warfare, emphasizing that diplomacy and strategic means like conciliation or bribery are preferable to the uncertainty of battle.</summary>
